Meta Announces $95 billion Stock Offering to Finance Expanding AI Infrastructure

29 Oct 2026, 07:34 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Tech Desk · Source: www.theguardian.com

4 min read

Key takeawaysThe company said the combined proceeds will support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence.” No specific timeline for the ATM program was given, but Meta indicated it will be launched after the underwritten tranche is completed.

Overview

Meta Platforms Inc., the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, disclosed a two‑part equity raise totalling $95 billion. The move is intended to fund the firm’s ongoing investment in artificial‑intelligence (AI) data centres and its broader “personal superintelligence” roadmap. The announcement arrived alongside public comments from Elon Musk warning that many smaller AI‑focused cloud providers – often called “neoclouds” – are facing severe funding shortages.

Details of the Fundraising

  • Phase 1 – Underwritten public offering: Meta will issue new shares worth $35 billion through a traditional underwritten sale. Chipmakers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have been identified as “cornerstone investors” and may purchase up to $5 billion of the offering.
  • Phase 2 – At‑the‑market (ATM) offering: A further $60 billion will be raised by selling newly created Class C common stock on an ongoing basis at prevailing market prices. Class C shares carry no voting rights, allowing Meta to raise capital without diluting Mark Zuckerberg’s control of the company.

The company said the combined proceeds will support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence.” No specific timeline for the ATM program was given, but Meta indicated it will be launched after the underwritten tranche is completed.

Why Meta Is Raising Capital

Meta has been expanding its AI compute capacity at a “multibillion‑dollar” pace, building new data‑centre sites and upgrading existing facilities. The firm’s recent earnings releases have highlighted AI as a core growth engine, but the capital‑intensive nature of the hardware (GPUs, networking equipment) and the need for large‑scale cooling and power infrastructure mean cash flow from operations alone may be insufficient to meet near‑term spending plans.

By issuing non‑voting Class C shares, Meta can tap public markets while preserving the existing governance structure that gives Zuckerberg a controlling stake. This approach mirrors similar dual‑class structures used by other tech giants to raise funds without ceding decision‑making power.

Industry Context: AI Debt Concerns

On the same day, Elon Musk posted on X that more than 200 neocloud providers are “facing guppy‑level death and consolidation” because debt markets have largely shut off financing for firms without substantial non‑AI revenue streams. He cited examples such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren, whose shares experienced volatility after his comments.

Analysts, including Neil Wilson of Saxo UK, have echoed Musk’s concerns, pointing to high leverage levels – for instance, CoreWeave reportedly carries about $35 billion in debt. By contrast, Meta’s balance sheet is strong, and the company can rely on equity raises rather than additional borrowing to fund its AI ambitions.

Practical Implications for Investors and Users

  • Investors: The underwritten offering may attract institutional buyers seeking exposure to AI‑related growth, while the ATM route offers a more gradual entry point for retail investors. The non‑voting nature of Class C shares means investors will not influence corporate governance, a factor to weigh against potential upside.
  • Meta users: The capital infusion is aimed at accelerating AI‑driven features across Meta’s platforms – from content recommendation algorithms to emerging “personal superintelligence” tools. Users could see faster rollout of new AI services, though the long‑term impact on privacy and data handling remains a subject of regulatory scrutiny.
  • Competitors: Smaller AI‑focused cloud providers may find it harder to compete for talent and hardware if larger players like Meta continue to pour billions into infrastructure.

What Remains Uncertain

  • Timing and pricing: Exact dates for the ATM offering and the price at which new shares will be sold are not disclosed. Market conditions could affect the amount ultimately raised.
  • Regulatory response: The creation of a new non‑voting share class may attract attention from securities regulators and shareholder‑rights advocates, especially given Meta’s history of antitrust scrutiny.
  • AI market growth: While Meta is confident in the demand for AI compute, the broader market’s ability to sustain the current level of investment – particularly for smaller providers – is still debated.

How to Verify

The full announcement and supporting details are available in Meta’s filing and the Guardian’s report published on 26 October 2026. Readers can review the original article at:

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/meta-plans-95bn-stock-offering-to-help-cover-ai-expansion

For the most up‑to‑date information, investors should also consult Meta’s investor‑relations website and any SEC filings related to the offering.
